extracted.intended_audience: educated readers of political biography, literary critics, and students of statesmanship
extracted.subtask_description: Observational guidance and evaluative criteria for writing and judging political/biographical essays and character sketches of statesmen, emphasizing qualities of authorship, memoir-writing, and the nature of constitutional statesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence should convey real feeling, not mechanical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Eloquence that reads or sounds like a machine — an 'incessant talking thing' or a 'gong going' — lacks real feeling and fails to move audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote of the old judge who mockingly called Brougham 'the Harangue' and misstated his speeches illustrates the anti-pattern: eloquence by machinery that is impressive in sound but not intelligible or felt. Prefer speech/writing that retains human feeling rather than mere rhetorical mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excitable, ungenial temperament limits abstract philosophical thought
rubrics_metrics.description: An excitable, ungenial nature incapacitates a man for abstract philosophy and deep consecutive reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although energetic and active minds may produce much writing, such temperament leads to works that are not of the 'first class' in subtle philosophy; an inquiring, brooding disposition is preferable for sustained philosophical argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brooding disposition and still investigating intellect are necessary for consecutive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The brooding disposition and the still investigating intellect are necessary for consecutive reasonings on delicate philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid alternation between subjects ('he who runs may read') prevents the deep thought and patient investigation needed for coherent philosophical work; writers should cultivate sustained attention for delicate arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid or hurried writing tends to inconsistency and confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Works produced hastily are likely to contain singular instances of inconsistency and confusion; 'he who runs may read, but it does not seem likely he will think.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why even numerous works on a subject may not be of the highest quality; care, deliberation, and slow thought reduce inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of information vs. depth — generalist knowledge has limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who is always changing subjects will know the outsides of many topics and possess immense information, but extreme correctness and painful acquaintance with any one subject cannot be expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General information is valuable but should not be mistaken for depth; critics should separate the merits of wide knowledge from the demands of exact scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: High information does not guarantee absolute correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a man of immense information cannot be expected to have extreme correctness in all matters; satire calling someone 'the most misinformed man in Europe' still implies compliment to his breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should allow for errors of detail in broadly informed writers while recognizing the value of wide learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest in physical science shapes generational intellects and temper
rubrics_metrics.description: An especial interest in physical science marks many impressible minds of the generation; advances in material civilization inspired sanguine hopes and influenced genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that scientific marvels can make life more superficial and that later generations may react against purely material studies; evaluators should consider how an author's scientific enthusiasms affect depth and moral seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'useful knowledge' (factish) from essential literature that moves the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Diffusing knowledge of useful things (dates, technical details, 'factish' knowledge) is not the same as producing literature that touches the heart and passions and contains an 'undefecated essence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations or works that focus on sheer material detail may successfully educate but fail to enrich inner life; critics should value literature and philosophy that stir love, hope, and character over mere accumulation of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memoirist's excellence lies in painting the exterior of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: As a memoirist, one may excel in sketching the exterior — the appearance and public conduct — of men encountered in law-courts and parliament, producing valuable portraits of political actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brougham's 'Statesmen of George III.' is cited as among the best sketches of political men; memoirists who observed men in action can be outstanding painters of character, even if they miss deeper inner essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best character sketches arise from direct personal encounter
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer's excellence in describing character is, in general, confined to men he had personally and keenly encountered; portraits of those not personally known (e.g., philosophers, foreign statesmen) may be poor and meagre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal experience and conflict sharpen observation; memoirists should rely on firsthand encounters rather than remote study for vivid sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partiality in memoirs toward one's youthful instructors is allowable
rubrics_metrics.description: An old man may be permitted to be over-partial and reverent in describing the instructors of his youth; such amiability is characteristic and not necessarily a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as an understandable exception to a memoirist's usual critical fairness; readers should note but not over-penalize such partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memoirs intended to show the subject's sincerity and conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal memoir may be designed to demonstrate that the actor sincerely believed his actions to be right — the focus being 'My Conscience' rather than national justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographers and memoirists often have the narrower aim of vindicating motives; critics should distinguish personal intent from broader political consequences when evaluating such works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional statesman = common opinions + uncommon abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional statesman is generally a man of common opinions and uncommon abilities because in free government one must persuade many persons and appeal to the average man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative criterion for political leadership: the ability to embody and express prevailing public sentiment while possessing administrative skill; originality that detaches from average opinion undermines electability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influential statesman expresses and administers the creed of the moment
rubrics_metrics.description: The most influential constitutional statesman felicitously expresses the creed of the moment, embodies it in laws and institutions, and induces the average man to accept it ('I could not have done it any better').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political success often depends on aligning with public sentiment and giving it institutional form; being first to the idea is less valued than making the idea practicable and acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion enforces conformity and punishes originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is a permeating influence that exacts obedience: those who deviate are labelled 'eccentric' or 'unsafe' and suffer career consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'tyranny of commonplace' is a political and social force; writers and politicians alike may hide intellect or conform to be accepted. Evaluators should recognize the social constraints shaping public figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesmen must be perceived as 'safe' and of sound judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: For public office, it is essential to be thought a man of judgment and to appear 'safe'; unlike literary men who may make bold claims safely, politicians' reputations depend on perceived prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral and administrative realities favor prudence and apparent reliability; boldness without reassurance is penalized by the electorate and peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political leadership often follows average opinion rather than leads it
rubrics_metrics.description: Many statesmen (exemplified by Peel) are converted to measures only when the average man has been converted; they often enter into labours after earlier advocates have done the hard pioneering work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical actors by whether they led change or consolidated it; being a consolidator has value but is distinct from pioneering reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different historical moments require different types of statesmen
rubrics_metrics.description: There are occasions when a statesman with prepared intelligence, distinct views, strong will and commanding mastery is required — times when mere administrators who echo popular opinion will not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should judge statesmen relative to the needs of their time: administrative skill is valuable in ordinary times; crises demand original, forceful leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective administration favors practical, hardworking managers over refined aristocrats
rubrics_metrics.description: The daily, enormous strain of government is usually borne by men of a lower grade — trained by early ambition, native aptitude, and hard competition — who are rough enough to accomplish business yet acquainted with higher classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts the aristocratic leisure that ill-suits daily administration with the practical competence of managers (e.g., Walpole-type figures); evaluators of statesmen should weigh practical administrative capacity heavily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memoirs risk reviving obsolete controversies and should be judged for that tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing memoirs that revive questions already settled (e.g., reviving the Catholic question) can be an error; such revivals may misrepresent the perspective of later generations and stir unnecessary debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographers and editors should be cautious about foregrounding controversies whose context has shifted; critics should note when memoirs reopen disputes without adding constructive insight.
